title: The Morning Brief: A weekend of natural disasters converges with legal and criminal news
dek: Hawaii braces for a rare hurricane landfall while Indonesia counts earthquake dead and Japan's record rains recede; separately, an NYPD conviction and a Somalia TPS ruling mark shifts in accountability and immigration law.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Multiple weather and geologic disasters are unfolding simultaneously across the Pacific and Midwest, while separate court rulings reshape immigration protections and police accountability.
bottom_line: Saturday's news is dominated by simultaneous natural disasters: a hurricane warning for Hawaii's Big Island as Tropical Storm Lala approaches, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake that killed at least 38 in eastern Indonesia, record rainfall deaths in Japan, and rising flood risk in the Midwest. Alongside these, a Boston judge lifted a stay on Somalia's TPS termination citing a Supreme Court ruling that narrowed judicial review, and an NYPD officer was convicted for the first time under the city's post-Floyd chokehold ban. The reporting documents these events and the legal reasoning behind the TPS ruling but does not resolve Lala's eventual track, the motives behind two separate shootings in Michigan and Virginia, or whether TPS plaintiffs have further recourse. Checkpoints ahead include updated hurricane advisories and Molokai's storm arrival Saturday, Indonesia's casualty updates, Japan's river levels through the weekend, and any arrests or motive disclosures in the Michigan and Virginia Sate University shootings.
body: The most concrete fact of the day: Hawaii's Big Island is under a hurricane warning as Tropical Storm Lala, packing 65 mph winds as of Friday evening, is forecast to reach hurricane strength and make landfall by Saturday, potentially dropping up to 25 inches of rain and a 3-foot storm surge. Hawaii Gov. Josh Green declared a state of emergency Thursday. It would be the state's first hurricane landfall since Category 4 Hurricane Iniki in 1992, which killed six people and caused $3 billion in damage. Separately, the National Weather Service Honolulu issued a Tropical Storm Warning for Molokai, forecasting peak winds of 35-45 mph gusting to 55 mph beginning Saturday afternoon.

Natural disasters dominate the wires beyond Hawaii. A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off eastern Indonesia's Flores region early Saturday, killing at least 38 people according to the National Disaster Management Agency, with a magnitude 6.9 aftershock following hours later; six others were injured and two remain missing. In eastern Japan, record rainfall, nearly three times the average August total according to the Japan Meteorological Agency, has killed at least eight people and cut power to more than 20,000 households in Chiba prefecture; the highest emergency alert was downgraded Friday as the deluge eased, though landslide and flooding risks persist. In the American Midwest, rivers are rising and threatening homes as severe weather continues, with NBC News reporting from outside Indianapolis on the growing flood danger.

On the legal and law enforcement side, NYPD officer Omar Habib was convicted Thursday of second-degree felony strangulation and violating New York City's 2020 chokehold ban, the first such conviction since the law was enacted after George Floyd's death. He faces up to seven years in prison and was terminated from the force. In Boston, U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs lifted a stay blocking the Trump administration's termination of Temporary Protected Status for Somali nationals, citing a June Supreme Court ruling in Mullin v. Doe that limited judicial review of TPS decisions. Burroughs found plaintiffs had presented a compelling case and would suffer irreparable harm, but concluded the Supreme Court's ruling constrained her authority. According to sources at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, 2,471 Somali nationals currently hold TPS, with another 1,383 applications pending.

Violence also marked the day: five people were killed across multiple scenes in rural Missaukee County, Michigan, Friday, with suspect Chad Hickman found dead in a wooded area after a manhunt; authorities have disclosed no motive. At Virginia State University, five people were shot early Saturday near student housing, one critically, days before the academic year was set to begin; multiple suspects are sought and no arrests have been announced. Separately, the FDA elevated a salmonella-linked egg recall to Class I, its highest risk category, covering 1.6 million cartons first recalled July 22 by Midwest Poultry Services.

The reporting does not explain why Lala's track remains uncertain beyond noting storms can shift, nor does it give a motive for the Michigan killings or the Virginia State University shooting. On the TPS ruling, the reporting establishes the legal mechanism, the Supreme Court's Mullin v. Doe precedent narrowing review, but does not say whether plaintiffs will pursue further appeals.
Desk boards were not available this cycle; the picture above rests entirely on today's published stories.

The coming days offer specific checkpoints. Hawaii: updated National Hurricane Center advisories through Saturday morning will refine Lala's track and intensity, with post-landfall damage assessments to follow; Molokai's tropical storm conditions are expected Saturday afternoon into early Sunday. Indonesia's disaster agency will update casualty and damage figures from the Flores earthquake. Japan's rainfall persistence and river-gauge readings over the weekend will show whether the crisis stabilizes or deepens. In Michigan and at Virginia State University, investigators are expected to release victim identities, motive, and any arrests. On the Somalia TPS case, watch for whether the administration sets a termination effective date and whether plaintiffs' remaining Fifth Amendment claims proceed in court.
